newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wholesale prices fell for fifth month in May.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wholesale prices fell for fifth month in May.

text.p: Wholesale prices fell in May for the fifth month in a row, the government said Friday, implying little or no inflation that would force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again next month.
The Labour Department said the Producer Price Index dropped 0.3 percent in May -- a surprise since economists had predicted a small increase -- marking the first string of five declines in 45 years.
"It's a great country!" exclaimed Edward Yardeni, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in New York, as analysts struggled to describe the latest stream of good economic news.

With Fed policy-makers scheduled to meet July 1-2 to weigh their next move on rates, most analysts said they expected the central bankers to hold steady with the economic news pointing to a slowdown in the second quarter.
"The economy seems to be engineering its own soft landing," said economist Bill Cheney of John Hancock Financial Services in Boston. "I can't see why the Fed will need to move any time soon."

After growing at a brisk 5.8 percent rate in the first quarter, the economy has shown more and more signs of slowing. Retail sales fell for the third straight month in May, the government reported on Thursday.

The strong first-quarter growth fanned inflation worries, and led the Fed to boost short-term rates in March for the first time in more than two years, so the slowdown now developing has been welcomed in financial markets, which rallied again after Friday's price report.

The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 73.73 points to 7,785.20 at midday, putting it in record territory for sixth straight session. The benchmark 30-year Treasury rose 21/32, or $6.56 on a $1,000 bond, sending its yield down to 6.72 percent from 6.78 percent Thursday.

A separate report from the Commerce Department showed stocks of unsold goods rose 0.3 percent in April, mainly because of a pileup on retail store shelves, a reflection of the slowdown in retail sales, which fell 0.1 percent in May.
While the sales report suggested consumers were bringing spending under control, consumer optimism remained buoyant.
A private University of Michigan survey Friday showed consumer confidence rose to 103.4 in June from an already-high 103.2 in May, people who saw the report said.
The drop in May producer prices followed a whopping 0.6 percent price decline in April. Excluding volatile food and energy costs, producer prices fell 0.3 percent after a 0.1 percent drop in April.

Robert Dederick, consulting economist to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago, said second-quarter growth would probably be at a 2 percent rate, or even slower. But he said growth was likely to pick up in the second half as inventories are worked off while spending for business expansion remained brisk.

"We are in what is going to be viewed in retrospect as one of the really golden eras of the U.S. economy," Dederick said, with the expansion in its seventh year and showing no sign of running out of steam.
Commerce Secretary William Daley, in an interview with Reuters, said the Clinton administration felt the economy was on a solid -- but slower -- growth track that was sustainable.
"I think it is going to continue, not the boom attitude, but just the solidness of this economy because it is based on some pretty good foundations," Daley said.

He said the economy should get another boost once a balanced-budget pact is finally worked out between the Republican-led Congress and the White House. The first major tax cut in more than 15 years as well as lower capital gains taxes are being negotiated.

The May decline in wholesale prices was led by another steep drop in energy costs. Gasoline prices in particular fell sharply, dropping by more than 7 percent, the biggest decline in more than 2-1/2 years.
Car prices fell 1.5 percent, the largest drop since October 1994. Computer prices fell 4.5 percent.
Wholesale food prices rose, however, with prices for beef, veal, fish and fruit all higher. Fruit prices jumped 8 percent with strawberry prices up 28 percent.

The report also showed there was not much inflation in the pipeline. Prices of intermediate goods, used to make finished wholesale products, fell 0.2 percent in May. But prices of crude goods, materials at the start of the production process, rose 1.3 percent after a 0.9 percent drop in April.
